title: Earth's Interior
intro: Nobody has ever been to the middle of Earth, so scientists work like doctors with an X-ray: they use earthquake waves, gravity, heat and magnetism to see inside. Learn the layers (chemical and physical), how seismic waves prove the outer core is liquid, and why the crust floats (isostasy).

learningObjectives.text: Explain how geologists investigate Earth's interior using indirect evidence.
Compare the crust, mantle, and core by composition and position.
Distinguish Earth's physical layers by their mechanical behavior.
Explain how density, pressure, and temperature change with depth inside Earth.
Compare P and S waves and explain how their speeds and paths change inside Earth.
Use seismic-wave shadow zones to infer the structure and liquid outer core of Earth.
Explain how gravity measurements relate to Earth's geoid and internal mass distribution.
Explain isostasy and how crustal density affects elevation.
Explain how internal heat drives mantle convection.
Describe how motion in Earth's outer core generates its magnetic field.
Explain how seismic reflection imaging reveals subsurface structure.

sections.title: How do we study a place we cannot visit?

boxes.text: Why so many probes? Firsthand information about the deep Earth is very limited. Each probe gives one clue, such as density from gravity or liquid versus solid from seismic waves. Put the clues together and you get the picture.
Think of guessing what is inside a wrapped gift: shake it (seismic), weigh it (gravity), feel it for warmth (heat flow), hold a magnet to it (magnetic field).

steps.title: Moment of inertia
bullets: **Moment of inertia** is about how Earth's rotation changes the shape of the planet, and how the planet responds to tides.

steps.title: Spheroidal oscillation
bullets: After a big earthquake Earth **rings like a bell**.
**Spheroidal** oscillation squeezes and stretches the planet in and out. The arrows show the outline moving in and out.

steps.title: Toroidal oscillation
bullets: **Toroidal** oscillation twists the two halves of the planet back and forth.
Both kinds are free oscillations: the whole Earth keeps ringing after a large quake.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Scientists use several **probes** (tools): samples, gravity and density, moment of inertia, free-body oscillations, heat flow, seismic studies, and the magnetic field.

Rock samples: **xenoliths** are chunks of deep rock carried up inside magma by volcanic eruptions. Most are **peridotite** (an ultramafic rock), so the mantle is thought to be mostly peridotite. Meteorites often contain more iron than surface rocks, which hints that Earth formed from similar material and that the core is mostly iron.

boxes.text: Why is the heavy stuff in the middle? Early Earth was partly molten. Heavy iron and nickel sank toward the centre, and light rock floated up to form the crust. Low-density materials float on top of higher-density materials.
Crust is like the skin of an apple, the mantle is the thick flesh, and the core is the pit. Density goes up as you go in: skin 2.7, flesh 3.3 to 5.7, pit 9.9 to 13.
Same idea, slightly different numbers. Remember 1 g/cm3 = 1000 kg/m3, and that density rises toward the centre. Also: oceanic crust is DENSER than continental crust, even though it is thinner.

head: Chemical layer
Made of
Density
Key facts
rows: Largest layer by volume, to ~2900 km

steps.title: Three chemical layers
bullets: The Earth is split into three **chemical layers** (by what they are made of): crust, mantle and core. Density goes up with depth: crust 2.7 to 3.3, mantle 3.3 to 5.7, core 9.9 to 13.0 g/cm3.

**Crust**: the thin outer skin. **Continental crust** is light and granite-like (felsic, intermediate and mafic rock), about 30 to 40 km thick. **Oceanic crust** is heavier and basalt-like (mafic rock), about 5 km thick.
**Mantle**: the biggest layer by volume, from the base of the crust to about 2900 km deep. Its rock is **ultramafic** (peridotite).

steps.title: Density rises toward the centre
bullets: The right half shows density in kg/m3 (1 g/cm3 = 1000 kg/m3): continental crust about 2700, mantle 3300 up to 5700, core roughly 9700 up to 16000.
Low-density materials float on top of higher-density materials, so the heavy stuff ended up in the middle.
**Core**: mostly **iron and nickel**, maybe a little oxygen. It has a liquid part and a solid part.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The **Moho** (Mohorovicic Discontinuity) is the boundary between crust and mantle. At the Moho, seismic wave speed jumps up because the rock chemistry changes.

Moho depth: about **5 km** below the sea floor under oceans, **30 to 40 km** under continents, and roughly **doubled** near big mountain belts. It was discovered by Andrija Mohorovicic in **1909** in Croatia.

sections.title: Physical layers: how each layer behaves

boxes.text: Why do geologists use two systems? Chemistry says WHAT the rock is. Physical layers say HOW it acts under stress. The asthenosphere is the same chemical stuff as the mantle below the lithosphere (peridotite) but is soft because it is hot, so it flows. That is why plates can glide over it.
Lithosphere = Lid (hard lid). Asthenosphere = Ass-of-the-lid, the soft, weak layer. Mesosphere = Middle stiff. Outer core = Over-liquid, inner core = Inside-solid.
The lithosphere is NOT the same as the crust: it includes the crust AND the uppermost mantle. The asthenosphere is NOT liquid magma: it is solid rock that flows very slowly (plastic).

head: Physical layer
State
Key behaviour
rows: Crust + top of mantle; broken into plates
Weak, flows; unbroken; has the LVZ
Lower mantle, more rigid than asthenosphere
Only fully liquid layer; makes magnetic field

steps.title: Lithosphere and the core
bullets: **Lithosphere** (about 100 km thick): solid and rigid. It is the crust plus the very top of the mantle, and it is broken into **plates**. Lithos means stone.
**Outer core**: the only entirely **liquid** layer. It starts about 2900 km down and ends at about 5150 km, so it is about 2300 km thick.
**Inner core**: **solid**, about 1220 km thick, with its top at about 5155 km depth.

steps.title: Asthenosphere, mesosphere and LVZ
bullets: **Asthenosphere** ('soft plastic'): weak and slowly flowing, right under the lithosphere. Astheno- means lacking strength. It is not broken into plates.

**Mesosphere** ('stiff plastic'): the stiffer lower mantle under the asthenosphere. The graph also marks the upper mantle, a **transition zone** (about 400 to 660 km) and the lower mantle (below 660 km).
**Low-velocity zone (LVZ)**: wave speed dips at about 100 to 200 km in the upper mantle, where the rock is weak and a little soft.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: The same Earth can also be split by **how the rock behaves** (solid and stiff, or soft and flowing). These are the **physical layers**.

sections.title: Density, pressure and temperature with depth
bullets: Both **pressure** and **temperature** increase from the surface to the centre. **Density** also increases toward the centre.

Graphs can plot temperature against depth. The **geotherm** (geothermal gradient) is the line showing how fast temperature rises with depth. A second line, the **melting curve**, shows when the rock would melt.

The graph labels: lithosphere, upper mantle (to ~410 km), lower mantle, solid silicate rock in the mantle, the **core-mantle boundary**, liquid iron alloy in the outer core, and solid iron alloy in the inner core.
The average gradient in the upper 100 km is about **25 degrees C per km**.
The inner core is the hottest part of Earth, yet it is **solid** because **enormous pressure** keeps the metal packed tight.

boxes.text: Why can the hottest place on Earth be solid? Melting needs room for atoms to move. Squeeze them with the weight of 5000 km of rock above and they cannot spread out into a liquid, even at very high temperature. Heat says 'melt', pressure says 'stay solid'. Pressure wins in the inner core.
Pressure cooker in reverse: squeezing keeps the metal solid, like packing a crowd so tightly nobody can move.

Exam wording: 'The inner core is solid because it is cooler' is WRONG. It is hotter than the outer core and solid because of pressure. Also the 25 degrees C per km figure is only for the upper ~100 km, not the whole Earth (textbook 4.3.1).

sections.title: Seismic waves: P, S, speed, bending

boxes.text: Why can P cross liquids but S cannot? A liquid can be squeezed and released (compression), so P gets through. But a liquid has no stiffness against sideways pushing: shear it and it just flows. With nothing pushing back, a side-to-side wave dies.
P = Push (and Primary, first to arrive). S = Shake sideways (and Secondary, second to arrive). Slinky: push-pull along it is P; flick it up and down is S.
Do NOT say 'S waves cannot go through the core'. They cannot go through the LIQUID OUTER core. Also 'P waves cannot go through liquids' is false: they can.

steps.title: P and S body waves
bullets: **Body waves** travel through the inside of Earth: **P waves** (primary, compression) and **S waves** (secondary, shear).
**P waves** push and pull rock forward and back, like sound. They are the **fastest** and travel through **solids AND liquids** (and gases).
**S waves** shake rock side to side. They are slower and travel only through **solids**. Where solid meets liquid the S waves stop, but the P wave keeps going.

steps.title: Wave fronts and rays
bullets: A quake at the **focus** sends out **wave fronts**. If the rock is the same everywhere, the fronts are circles in cross-section.
A **seismic ray** is a line showing the path of the wave, at right angles to the front.

steps.title: Waves spreading through the mantle
bullets: Wave fronts spread out from the focus through the crust and into the mantle.
A ray from the source can reflect off the core and reach a **seismometer** (the instrument that records waves).

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Waves are faster in denser, stronger rock: the same wave goes farther in **basalt** than in **sandstone** in the same time.

At a boundary a ray is partly **reflected** (bounces back) and partly **refracted** (bends). Going into a slower layer the ray bends toward the vertical; into a faster layer it bends away. Because speed rises smoothly with depth, rays follow a smooth curve and come back up to the surface.

sections.title: What waves reveal: shadow zones and the liquid core

boxes.text: Why does this prove the outer core is liquid? S waves cannot cross liquid. A whole region on the far side gets no S waves. So something liquid must be in the way, and its size and depth match the outer core. Lehmann later (1936) used wave paths to show a solid inner core sits inside it.
S for Sorry, can't Swim: S waves cannot swim through liquid. P for Passes everything.

Mix-up pair: the S-wave shadow zone (everything beyond ~103 degrees) shows the outer core is LIQUID. The P-wave shadow zone (103 to 143 degrees) is caused by BENDING at the core. It is not a 'no P waves allowed' zone.

head: Shadow zone
Where
What it shows
rows: P waves bend at core-mantle boundary

steps.title: P-wave shadow zone
bullets: The **P-wave shadow zone** is a band from about **103 to 143 degrees** from the quake where few direct P waves arrive.
P waves are bent (refracted) as they enter the core, leaving a ring-shaped gap.

steps.title: S-wave shadow zone
bullets: In the **S-wave shadow zone**, no S waves arrive anywhere beyond about **103 degrees**, all the way round to the other side.
They are stopped by the **liquid outer core**, so this whole far-side zone maps out the outer core.

steps.title: Seismic tomography
bullets: **Seismic tomography** builds maps of the inside of Earth from wave speeds.
Colour key: **blue = slower**, **red = faster** waves. The 3-D cut-away shows the mantle, outer core and inner core.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Seismic velocities generally increase with depth**, with some drops. The speed jumps at the base of the crust (the Moho), dips in the **low-velocity zone (LVZ)** at about 100 to 200 km, then steps up at the transition zone (about 400 to 660 km).

On a velocity-versus-depth graph, at the **core-mantle boundary (about 2900 km)** the P-wave speed drops sharply and the S-wave line stops. In the outer core only P is shown. In the **inner core** (below about 5155 km) both a P and an S line appear.

boxes.text: Why is it bumpy? Where there is extra mass underground, gravity is a bit stronger and the uniform-gravity surface rises. Where mass is missing it dips. So the bumps are a map of density differences below.
The correct definition is the surface of uniform gravity.

steps.title: Sphere, spheroid and geoid
bullets: Three shapes are compared: a perfect **sphere**, a **spheroid** (a ball slightly flattened by rotation) and the **geoid** (a bumpy surface). On the 3-D globe, highs are red and lows are blue.
The **geoid** is the **surface of uniform gravity** on Earth. It is roughly sea level extended under the continents.

steps.title: Map of geoid height
bullets: This map shows geoid height, from about **-100 m to +50 m** (blue lows, red highs).

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Gravity varies slightly because mass is not spread evenly. That is why the geoid is lumpy, and why gravity is a probe of density.

sections.title: Isostasy: crust floats on the mantle

boxes.text: Why does the land rise after ice melts? The ice pushed the crust down and the asthenosphere flowed aside. When the ice goes, the asthenosphere flows back in very slowly (it is thick, soft rock), so the rebound takes thousands of years and is still going on.
A boat or an iceberg: most of an iceberg is underwater. Take off cargo and the boat bobs up; load it and it sinks.

Rebound is slow and steady, NOT during earthquakes only, and it is NOT sinking after the ice melts. Land is rising because the weight is gone, not sinking because water replaced the ice. Also, the thickest crust is under big mountain ranges, not under ocean ridges.

steps.title: A cargo ship floats like crust
bullets: With an empty hold the ship rides high (large **freeboard**). Fill the hold and it sinks lower. Earth's crust works the same way.
Add a heavy **load** (mountain, ice sheet) and the crust sinks into the asthenosphere. Remove the load (ice melts, erosion) and the crust slowly floats back up. That is **isostatic rebound**.
After the last ice age (about 19,000 years ago), Canada and Scandinavia are still rising. Hudson Bay is a classic example.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: **Isostasy** is the balance of floating crust on the mantle. Continental lithosphere is lower in density than the asthenosphere, so it is buoyant.
Thick crust under big mountain belts (Moho depth about doubled) is another case of floating: a heavy block sinks deeper.

boxes.text: Why does hot rock rise? Heat makes rock expand and so become a little less dense. Lighter rock floats up, cools at the top, becomes denser and sinks. Like a pot of soup, but incredibly slow. This stirring pushes the plates along (and supplies the energy for plate tectonics).
Heat sources: 'Left-over plus Leaking' = leftover heat from formation plus radioactive leakage (decay).

The Sun does NOT power mantle convection. Sunlight only warms the surface. Practice midterm answer: radioactive decay plus heat left over from Earth's formation. Friction at plate boundaries and Moon tides are not the main energy source.

steps.title: Convection loops inside Earth
bullets: Heat flows out. Hot rock rises and cooler rock sinks in loops called **convection cells**. The arrows show these cells inside the mantle and the outer core.
The asthenosphere flows because of **convection currents** created by heat from Earth's core.

steps.title: Cells, plate graveyard and plume
bullets: **Convecting cell**: one of the loops where hot rock rises and cooler rock sinks.
**Plate graveyard?** marks where cold plates may sink deep into the mantle (the question mark means it is a guess).
**Mantle plume**: a rising column of hot rock.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Earth's interior is hot from two main sources: **residual heat** left over from Earth's formation, and ongoing **radioactive decay**. Early heat came from gravitational compression, radioactive decay and asteroid impacts.
The inner core slowly grows as the outer core freezes onto it when heat escapes.

sections.title: Magnetic field and the outer core

boxes.text: Why does a moving liquid make a magnetic field? Metal that conducts electricity, stirred around, makes electric currents, and currents make a magnetic field. This is why only the liquid outer core matters. A frozen core would give no field.

Magnetic poles are not the same as geographic (rotation-axis) poles. The pole positions change, and the field has flipped many times (reversals). 'Moving poles show that the flow in the outer core changes with time' is the idea to remember.

steps.title: Outer core and reversal stripes
bullets: The rate of convection in the outer core determines, in part, what kind of rocks are deposited on the continents.
The striped columns are the **magnetic reversal timescale**: black and white stripes for normal and reversed polarity, grouped into **chrons** (Brunhes, Matuyama, Gauss, Gilbert).
If the outer core stopped moving or solidified, the field would disappear and the planet would lose gases and water, as happened on Mars.

steps.title: The north magnetic pole is racing
bullets: The north magnetic pole has been **wandering**: it is moving away from Canada toward Siberia.
Its speed has increased in recent decades (the graph is labelled 'Rapid Pole Shift').
The picture asks 'Reversal?': could the field flip? It has flipped many times before.

steps.title: Wandering poles
bullets: The maps trace where the north and south magnetic poles have been over the years.
The graph shows the north pole's speed staying low for most of the 1900s, then climbing to roughly 55 km per year in the 2000s.
Moving poles show that the flow in the outer core changes with time.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: Earth acts like a giant bar magnet. The north **magnetic** pole is not at the north **geographic** pole: they are about **8 degrees** apart. The field is generated by **circulating molten iron and nickel in the outer core**.
A magnetic anomaly map of the **Midcontinent Rift (MCR)** shows up to **15 km of basalt**. Rock with different magnetism shows up as colour (negative to positive).

boxes.text: Why two-way time? The pulse goes down, bounces, and comes back. The clock measures the round trip. Deeper layers take longer.
Seismic reflection uses a human-made source, not an earthquake. The vertical axis is time, not depth. (Oil use is outside source.)

steps.title: A reflection cross-section
bullets: Echoes are recorded and drawn as a cross-section, with **two-way travel time** (in seconds) on the vertical axis instead of depth.
The wavy bands are rock layers (strata), so you can see their folds.

steps.title: Collecting the data
bullets: A ship tows **air guns** that send a pulse of energy through the water into the layers below.
On land, large trucks **thump the Earth** instead.

steps.title: Key points
bullets: This is how geologists see layers and folds in the crust, for example to look for oil.

quiz.q: What is the geoid?
options: The surface of uniform gravity on Earth
A surface of constant Earth radius
Earth's surface adjusted for the centrifugal effect
quiz.why: The geoid is the surface of uniform gravity. It is lumpy because mass is not spread evenly, so it is not a constant-radius surface.

quiz.q: The S-wave shadow zone shows that one of Earth's layers is liquid. Which layer?
quiz.why: S waves cannot pass through liquid, so the region where they are missing outlines the liquid outer core.

quiz.q: Seismic wave velocities in the Earth...?
quiz.why: Density and velocity generally rise with depth, which is why rays curve back to the surface (with some dips like the LVZ).

quiz.q: S-waves do not pass through the outer core. What does this tell us?
options: The outer core is hotter than the inner core
The outer core is made of silicate rock
The outer core is solid iron
The outer core is liquid, and S-waves cannot travel through liquids
S-waves are too slow to reach the core
quiz.why: Shear waves need a solid to push against. A liquid cannot carry them, so a missing S-wave zone means liquid.

quiz.q: Which statement about Earth's interior is NOT correct?
options: The Moho separates the crust from the mantle
The lithosphere includes the crust and the uppermost mantle
The inner core is solid even though it is extremely hot, because of enormous pressure
Oceanic crust is denser than continental crust
The asthenosphere is mostly liquid magma
quiz.why: The asthenosphere is solid rock that is soft and flows slowly, not liquid magma. The other four statements are correct.

quiz.q: Where is Earth's crust thickest?
options: Beneath large mountain ranges such as the Himalayas and Tibet
Beneath hotspot volcanoes in the ocean
quiz.why: Oceanic crust is about 5 km thick, continental 30 to 40 km, and near large mountain belts the Moho depth is roughly doubled.

quiz.q: Thousands of years after a thick ice sheet melted off the Hudson Bay region, what is the land surface doing?
options: Sinking, because the mantle is cooling
Rising slowly, as the lithosphere rebounds isostatically
Sinking, because water replaced the ice
quiz.why: The ice pushed the crust down into the asthenosphere. With the load gone, the crust floats slowly back up (isostatic rebound), which is still happening in Canada.

quiz.q: Where does the energy that drives mantle convection and plate tectonics mainly come from?
options: Radioactive decay plus heat left over from Earth's formation
quiz.why: Earth's interior heat comes from leftover formation heat and radioactive decay. Sunlight warms only the surface, so (e) is wrong.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about seismic body waves:
I. P waves are compressional and can travel through solids and liquids. II. S waves are shear waves that move rock side to side. III. P waves are slower than S waves.
quiz.why: I and II are true. P waves are the fastest body waves, so III is false.

quiz.q: Why do seismic rays curve back up toward the surface instead of travelling in straight lines?
options: Because the core reflects every ray
Because S waves are slower than P waves
Because gravity pulls the rays down
Because wave velocity generally increases with depth, so rays are refracted away from the vertical
quiz.why: Density increases with depth, velocity increases with density, and refraction keeps bending the ray back toward the surface.

quiz.q: Which statement best explains the P-wave shadow zone between about 103 and 143 degrees?
options: P waves cannot travel through liquids
P waves are absorbed completely by the crust
S waves interfere with the P waves
P waves bend (refract) at the core-mantle boundary, where their speed changes
The inner core stops all P waves
quiz.why: P waves can travel through liquid, so (a) is false. P speed drops at the core-mantle boundary and P waves are refracted there, leaving a ring-shaped gap.

quiz.q: The inner core is the hottest part of Earth, yet it is solid. Why?
options: It is cooler than the outer core
Immense pressure keeps its metal in a solid phase
It is made of silicate rock
It is too far from the Sun to melt
quiz.why: Heat alone would melt it, but the extreme pressure of the overlying layers keeps it solid.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT one of the physical layers of the Earth?
quiz.why: The crust is a chemical layer (with mantle and core). Physical layers are lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere, outer core and inner core.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements about the Moho:
I. It is the boundary between crust and mantle, marked by a jump in seismic velocity. II. It was discovered by Andrija Mohorovicic in 1909. III. It lies about 5 km below the ocean floor and about 30 to 40 km below the continents.
quiz.why: All three are true: a velocity jump at the crust base, discovered in 1909 in Croatia, 5 km under the ocean and 30 to 40 km under the continents.

quiz.q: If temperature rises about 25 degrees C per km in the upper crust, about how much hotter is the rock 8 km down than at the surface?
quiz.why: 8 km x 25 degrees C per km = 200 degrees C.

quiz.q: An empty ship floats high and a loaded ship floats lower. What is the equivalent for a continent when a thick ice sheet grows and later melts?
options: The continent rises when the ice grows, then sinks when it melts
The continent does not move at all
The crust sinks into the asthenosphere under the load, then rebounds upward after melting
quiz.why: The ice is the cargo. More weight pushes the crust down into the asthenosphere, and when the weight is removed the crust floats back up slowly.

quiz.q: Which layer's circulation of molten iron and nickel is believed to generate Earth's magnetic field?
quiz.why: The field is generated by circulation of molten iron and nickel in the outer core. Only the outer core is liquid.

quiz.q:
Consider these statements:
I. The lithosphere includes the crust and the uppermost mantle. II. The asthenosphere is broken into plates just like the lithosphere. III. The asthenosphere flows because of convection.
quiz.why: The asthenosphere is relatively unbroken, so II is false. I and III are true.

quiz.q: Earth's magnetic north pole has wandered, and the field has reversed in the past. What does this tell us?
options: The magnetic field is fixed to the crust
The inner core has stopped spinning
The flow in the outer core changes over time
quiz.why: The field comes from outer-core circulation, so a changing field means the flow is changing.

quiz.q: Which order lists Earth's chemical layers from LEAST dense to MOST dense?
options: They all have the same density
quiz.why: Crust is 2.7 to 3.3, mantle 3.3 to 5.7, core 9.9 to 13.0 g/cm3. Density rises toward the centre.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the probes of Earth's interior?
options: Drilling a hole to the core
quiz.why: The probes are samples (xenoliths, intrusions, meteorites), gravity, moment of inertia, oscillations, heat flow, seismic and magnetic probes. Nobody has drilled to the core.
